Make the face reveal less literal: the portrait-in-particles beat is a well-worn trope, so give it a twist or a reason tied to the subject
Push composition beyond centred symmetrical fields; several frames are mirror-balanced and read as algorithm defaults

tells: A cut-paper visual language in the Matisse tradition, carried all the way through: flat organic leaves and corals with grain stippling inside the fills, not default vector fills

A clear narrative idea about looking and desire: a peeping character making binoculars with his hands, the 'Melones' poster gag, a tongue close-up, and then the 'BLANC VOYEUR club' neon sign as the payoff
The typography is varied and has character: retro 3D shadowed script for 'Melones', hand-drawn neon lettering with a script 'club' tail, and a mix of faces that fits the scene
A deliberate primary palette (pink-red, cobalt, mustard, emerald on white or black) that inverts into neon on black for the finale
The scale changes from frame to frame (wide foliage, mid-shot character, poster, extreme close-up of lips, sign), which points to edited choreography rather than one repeated layout
The character design is asymmetric and has wit, and does not look like clip art
gaps: Light is mostly flat graphic fill. Only the neon frame uses real glow, so the reveal could be pushed with light bleeding back into the earlier scenes
The cheeky innuendo (melons, tongue) is a familiar illustration-reel trope. It needs a sharper or more surprising turn to reach best-of-year
The foliage-burst opener is close to a widespread trend in editorial illustration and could be more ownable

tells: Built from photogrammetry or point-cloud scans of real streets, bent into tunnels, a kaleidoscopic rosette of houses and spiky terrain: a specific medium explored on purpose
Dense, layered frames with real scanned texture, deliberate corruption and red channel-shifting, plus a burning sunset sky in the inverted-city shot
Spoken or monologue text is projected as scattered monospace glyphs along a voxel corridor and integrated with the space, not laid on top like a slide
Strong variety across frames (red tunnel, mesh terrain, polar inversion, text corridor, collapsing street), which suggests a camera journey with escalating distortion
gaps: The glitch/datamosh look sits close to the house style of many point-cloud art pieces. It needs a stronger authorial frame to stand out
The palette swings between saturated red and natural sky without an obvious system, so some frames read as accidental rather than designed
The text corridor uses a default monospace. Treating that type with a real point of view would lift the most conceptual moment

gaps: Voronoi-from-video is a stock creative-coding technique. It needs a specific idea or subject only this piece could own
The grey-on-grey tonal range is flat. It needs real light, contrast design or a deliberate accent to give the frames poster value

defects: Frame 4 (~10s) is close to black. It shows only a faint window glyph on a dark field, which is more than 1 s of dead air with no visible purpose.

The 'WE WERE NEVER MEANT TO STAY' card abandons the bulb-letter device for flat, dark, solid type on a grey noise field. The text is low-contrast and reads as murky rather than intentional, and 'TO STAY' is cut off by the frame edge and a horizontal wipe line.

At the 100% crop the bulbs are smeared into horizontal chevron streaks: directional smear stands in for real motion blur, there are no clean point-light cores, and the letterforms break down into noise.
The water background is a soft, horizontally stretched noise plate with no specular highlights or depth. Shadows show compression mush and banding.
Word reveals are hard on/off pops ('LOW' → 'LOW TIDE'), with no stagger, flicker-on or light build.
The 'lights are gone' reveal is a flat horizontal wipe with a vertical-line artefact at the wipe edge. It is not a light-by-light extinguish.
The reflections under the type are a crude vertical smear that doesn't match the water surface in frame 1.
Shots run up to 8.2 s with mostly static camera framing. Several seconds barely change from the previous second.
gaps: Motion: the main device (lyrics spelled in harbour lights) is never choreographed. The film needs lights that ignite in sequence, flicker, sway on the swell and go dark one by one on 'gone', plus a camera that drifts across the harbour. As it stands, words pop on and wipe off over static plates, with no easing, overlap or arc toward a peak.

Finish: the bulbs should read as real point lights, with crisp cores, bloom falloff, true reflections broken up by the water and clean motion blur. Instead the plates are smeared, banded and noisy. The material shift in the middle (solid dark type on grey noise) breaks the visual rule rather than reading as a deliberate counterpoint.

Sound and picture: the track is produced music with a real section change near 3 s and a dip near 7 s, plus two broadband hits near 13 s and 15.9 s. Picture events don't visibly land on them, though: there is no light-out on a hit and no cut on the downbeat. The film runs as a lyric slideshow over the song instead of being cut to it.
